comments.author: simonw
comments.text:
I think there's a material difference between being a meat proxy (great term) as defined in this article and working at a company where most code is written by agents.

Most of the code I produce is written by agents now, and I feel completely engaged with the process. I'm also careful not to forward agent slop onto other humans: slop is allowed in branches, but by the time it needs review by someone else or lands on main it needs to not be a waste of time for another human to look at it.

What this means is still shaping up. I expect a lot of coding agent users haven't found a great balance yet - I'm still trying to find the right balance myself.

Fundamentally though I believe that being a meat proxy or a slop canon is a choice, and so is choosing to produce lower quality work faster using AI. We can chose differently. I think employers that try to enforce the lower-quality-but-faster thing will soon be outcompeted by companies that chose higher-quality-and-faster.

comments.author: hjvt
comments.text:
That's an incredible way to miss the point, your shot landed on a whole different planet to the barn wall I've put up.



I don't want to drink leaded gasoline




Have you considered that guzzling leaded gasoline is not necessary? You can just tastefully sip it through a straw! And moreover, we are yet to figure out the health implications, and I just love the extra performance my car gets!


Anyways.


I think employers that try to enforce the lower-quality-but-faster thing will soon be outcompeted by companies that chose higher-quality-and-faster.


The low-quality-but-faster has already been winning for pretty much as long as software existed, why would you expect that to change now that you can go even lower, and even faster, and also reduce head counts?

The only way this can change, is if the whole economic system that's incentivizing this way of doing business collapses, or is forced to change by regulatory pressure.

comments.author: simonw
comments.text:
The low-quality-but-faster has already been winning for pretty much as long as software existed, why would you expect that to change now that you can go even lower, and even faster, and also reduce head counts?


Because it's so much cheaper now to do things well.

Teams used to skip out on automated tests and good documentation and experimental prototypes and load tests and security reviews because each of those things took significant time, and software engineering is fundamentally about deciding how to invest the limited time resource that is available to your team.

The time needed for all of those things has dropped - and the value provided by those things increases the faster you want to go.

Smart companies can chose to invest their resources in practices that help them ship better software, faster.

(And yeah, if your starting position is that using coding agents is equivalent to drinking gasoline I'm afraid this profession may be a frustrating place for you over the next few years.)

comments.author: laurentbroy
comments.text:
Maybe there is some cynicism in me, but I think for some sort of discussion in the corporate world, an LLM answering in my stead may not be that bad.

You know the kind. Your non-technical project manager poke you on Team on a Friday afternoon, and start asking you if you will be done by today, it is obvious that you won't because there are still several days of work remaining. So the PM ask you to justify why you are not done, and no matter what your answer, the discussion go downhill because the "the team must commit to finish what it promise to deliver", and he can't understand that you can't think faster than you are doing now.

Nothing I would like more than to plug an LLM on all the classic book on project management, on the nature of probability, and the notes I took on my current issue; and let that LLM very patiently explain to my manager the nature of uncertainty and of risk management and how no matter what someone promise (or more exactly, have been forced to promise) reality always win in the end, and reading through my note, demonstrating that I have in fact been working hard, and despite that hard work, there is still no chance whatsoever the issue will be resolved within 2 hours. Which will likely result in a request for overtime but that would have happened anyway.

Depending on how much of a corporate drone the PM is, that may or may not go over his head, but at least I wouldn't lose my time (and my temper) talking to a brick wall.
